about.title: Corona Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Corona sits where SR-91 meets I-15, and a lot of what fills local homes, garages and job sites arrives by truck along those routes. Most of it works as intended. Some of it does not. A space heater that ignites, a child's car seat that fails on the freeway, a power tool whose guard slips, a medication with warnings that left something out — these are the kinds of harms California's product liability law was built to address. The rule is different from an ordinary negligence claim. Under strict liability, you generally do not have to prove the manufacturer was careless. You show the product had a design, manufacturing or warning defect, and that the defect caused your injury. Responsibility can reach the maker, the distributor and the store in Corona that sold it. What matters most right now is simple: keep the product. Do not repair it, return it or throw it away. We handle product liability claims on contingency for Riverside County residents, so there is no fee unless you recover.

items.desc: The item that hurt you is the center of the case, and once it is returned, repaired or discarded, the defect can be nearly impossible to show. We help you understand what to keep and how to keep it before anything is lost.

items.title: Every Link in the Chain Considered
items.desc: California allows claims against manufacturers, distributors and retailers, including a Corona store that sold the product. We can look at the whole chain, and work on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: My airbag didn't deploy in a crash on SR-91 in Corona. Is that a car accident case or a product case?
items.answer: It can be both. Corona recorded 735 injury collisions in 2025, and in some of those, a safety system that should have worked did not. If a seat belt, airbag or tire failed, a strict liability claim against the manufacturer may exist alongside any claim against another driver. Keep the vehicle from being scrapped or repaired until an attorney has looked at it.

items.question: Do I have to prove the company knew the product was faulty?
items.answer: Generally, no. California's strict liability rule means you show the product was defective in its design, manufacture or warnings and that the defect caused your injury. The maker's state of mind is usually not the question. That is a meaningful difference from a standard negligence claim.

items.question: I bought it at a store in Corona but it was made overseas. Who can I actually hold responsible?
items.answer: California law lets injured people pursue manufacturers, distributors and retailers, so the local seller is often part of the picture even when the maker is hard to reach. We can sort out which parties are realistic to pursue. Hold on to the receipt, packaging and the product itself, since those help trace the chain of distribution.
